key_terms.meaning: Building a solid part by adding material layer upon layer from a 3D CAD model, instead of removing material from a block.
Making each unit different to the customer's order at near mass-production cost, with no extra tooling per design.
Standard exchange file that describes only the outer surface of the model as a mesh of small flat triangles.
Cutting the STL model into thin horizontal cross-sections of thickness h; number of layers N = part height ÷ h.
The direction in which the part sits on the build platform; it fixes layer plane, build height, support need and surface finish.
All work after the build: support removal, cleaning, UV curing, sanding, machining, heat treatment or painting.
A liquid resin whose short molecular chains join into a solid network when exposed to ultraviolet light.
AM process that scans a UV laser or projector over a liquid photopolymer bath and cures one cross-section at a time.
The internal pattern of a built part, given as a percentage of solid density; 100% infill means a completely solid interior.
Thickness of one extruded layer in mm; smaller h gives a smoother surface but more layers and a longer build.
Angle between the deposited roads and the part axis, usually 0° or 45°; alternating ±45° gives a cross-hatch pattern.
Extra material printed under overhangs and free spaces, then broken away, because a layer needs material below it.
AM family in which a thin powder layer is spread, then a laser or electron beam fuses only the chosen cross-section.
PBF process where the laser heats polymer or metal powder enough to sinter the particles, without fully melting them.
AM process that feeds metal powder through a nozzle into a laser melt pool on a substrate, with no powder bed.
Pattern in which successive sheet layers are laid at right angles or alternating directions so the bonded stack behaves evenly in both directions.
Removing the surplus sheet material cut into a block pattern around the part after laminated object manufacturing.
AM process where a printhead squirts liquid binder into a powder bed to glue the chosen cross-section; the part is later cured or sintered.
Using AM to make moulds, dies, inserts or patterns, so a tool is ready in days instead of weeks.
Using AM to make the final end-use part itself, not a model or a tool.

takeaways: Additive manufacturing adds material layer by layer from a 3D model, so it needs no part-specific tooling and can make internal channels that machining cannot reach.
AM processes are classified by how the layer is formed: liquid resin cured, filament melted, powder fused, sheet bonded, or droplets jetted.
The AM chain is fixed: CAD model, STL export, orientation, slicing, layer-by-layer build, then post-processing.
Stereolithography gives the finest surface finish but needs supports and a photopolymer that is weak and sensitive to sunlight.
Fused deposition modelling is the cheapest and simplest AM route, and layer height, raster angle and infill set the trade-off between time, strength and finish.
Powder bed fusion supports the part in loose powder, so overhangs need no extra support and one build can nest many parts.
LENS builds or repairs metal parts by blowing powder into a laser melt pool, and is used on shafts, dies and turbine blades rather than on a powder bed.
Laminated object manufacturing bonds and cuts sheets, giving low cost and large size but poor internal features after de-cubing.
Jetting processes split into material jetting, which deposits and cures liquid droplets, and binder jetting, which glues powder with a printed binder.
Rapid tooling and rapid manufacturing extend AM from prototypes to moulds and to end-use parts, which pays off for low volume and mass customisation.
bank_note: Long answers are expected to explain each process with a neat labelled sketch, list advantages and limits, compare two processes on material, accuracy, speed and cost, and end with a named industrial application.

bank.q: Define additive manufacturing. Explain how AM processes are classified, and list the advantages of AM over conventional subtractive manufacturing.
outline: Definition: material added layer by layer from a 3D model
Classification by layer formation: liquid photopolymer cured, thermoplastic extruded, powder fused, sheet bonded, droplets jetted
Classification by material state and by energy source (laser, electron beam, heat, UV)
Advantages: no part-specific tooling, complex internal channels, low-volume production, mass customisation, less waste
Limits mentioned briefly: slow for large quantities, size limits, post-processing, material cost

bank.q: Explain the rapid prototyping process chain from CAD model to finished part, stating what happens at each step.
outline: CAD model built in solid modeller
Export to STL; effect of chord height and triangle size
Orientation choice and its effect on build height, supports and finish
Slicing into layers of thickness h; N = height ÷ h
Layer-by-layer build with the machine toolpath
Post-processing: support removal, cleaning, curing, finishing
Process planning: check for undercuts, minimum feature size, shrinkage allowance

bank.q: Describe stereolithography with a neat sketch. State its advantages, limitations and applications.
outline: Liquid photopolymer vat, build platform that lowers by one layer, UV laser with galvo scanner or DLP projector
Curing of one cross-section, then platform moves down by layer thickness and resin recoats
Supports needed for overhangs; drain and post-cure after building
Advantages: fine feature size, smooth surface, good accuracy
Limits: photopolymer brittle, UV-sensitive, costly resin, supports leave marks
Applications: dental models, hearing-aid shells, jewellery patterns, visual prototypes

bank.q: Explain fused deposition modelling with a neat sketch. Define layer height, raster angle, infill and support, and state how each affects the part.
outline: Filament driven by drive wheels, heated liquefier, nozzle of small diameter, X-Y motion, platform moves down by h
Roads laid side by side; alternating ±45° raster gives cross-hatch
Layer height h: smaller h means smoother but more layers and longer time
Infill percentage controls weight, strength and time
Support material for overhangs and bridges, removed later
Advantages (cheap, safe, office-friendly) and limits (weak layer bonding, rough surface, slow for large parts)

bank.q: Explain powder bed fusion with reference to selective laser sintering. Include the build cycle, the role of loose powder, and the main advantages and limits.
outline: Recoater spreads a thin powder layer; laser scans only the cross-section
Platform drops by one layer; next layer spread; repeat
Loose powder supports overhangs, so no separate supports and parts can be nested
Sintering versus full melting (SLS versus SLM); materials: nylon, TPU, steel, aluminium, titanium
Advantages: strong functional parts, no support removal, batch builds
Limits: rough surface, porosity, thermal distortion, expensive machine and powder handling

bank.q: Describe laminated object manufacturing with a neat sketch. Explain the roles of the supply roll, heated roller, cutting head, take-up roll and de-cubing.
outline: Sheet on supply roll; heated roller bonds it to the stack below
Cutting head traces the cross-section outline; interior cut into cross-hatch squares for easy removal
Platform drops by sheet thickness and the next sheet is fed
Take-up roll collects the used backing
Build block removed and de-cubed by hand
Advantages: cheap sheets, large parts, no supports, no distortion; limits: internal features poor, paper absorbs moisture, finish depends on sheet edge

bank.q: A hydraulic manifold for a racing team needs curved internal cooling channels that no drill can reach, and only 20 pieces are needed. Choose an AM process, justify the choice, and state the post-processing needed.
outline: Requirement: internal channels, low volume, no tooling
Compare SLS/SLM, SLA and FDM on channel clearance, strength and cost
Metal PBF or SLM chosen for pressure-tight metal manifold; note need to drain and clean internal powder
Post-processing: powder removal, stress relief, support removal, machining of sealing faces, pressure test
Unsupported internal channels cannot be made by CNC drilling, so AM is the correct route

bank.q: A cube of side 40 mm is built by FDM with layer height 0.2 mm, raster width 0.4 mm and 20% infill. Explain step by step how you would estimate build time, and state which factors make the real time longer than the estimate.
outline: Volume of material = solid volume × infill fraction plus shell and supports
Deposited volume divided by volumetric flow rate of nozzle gives ideal time
Number of layers N = height ÷ h = 40 ÷ 0.2 = 200 layers
Add travel moves, layer change time, acceleration and retraction
Real time longer because of supports, raft, slow first layer, small features and machine limits
Conclusion: time scales with 1/h, so doubling h roughly halves the number of layers

bank.q: A start-up in Chennai must make 50 identical plastic enclosures with a smooth visible surface. Compare SLA, FDM and SLS for this batch and recommend one, giving reasons.
outline: SLA: best surface, brittle resin, supports on the visible face may spoil finish
FDM: cheapest, layer lines visible, weakest in the build direction
SLS: strong nylon, no supports, uniform surface, higher cost per part
For 50 units all three are economical because no tooling is needed; compare cost per part and finish
Recommendation with reason, plus post-processing (bead blasting, painting, tapping inserts)

bank.q: A worn die insert of an injection mould is to be restored instead of replaced. Explain how LENS would be used, step by step, and state the checks needed after repair.
outline: Worn surface machined back to sound metal
Substrate mounted; laser forms a small melt pool; metal powder blown into it through a nozzle
Nozzle and laser trace the path layer by layer, building up the lost volume
Controlled atmosphere to avoid oxidation; low heat input limits distortion
Post-repair: stress relief, machining to final size, hardness check, dye-penetrant inspection
Reason for choice: repair of a large existing part, no powder bed needed

bank.q: A mould for 5000 injection-moulded toy parts is needed quickly. Explain how rapid tooling would be used, naming the AM route and the steps from pattern to first moulding.
outline: Rapid tooling means AM makes the tool, not the part
Options: SLA or SLS master pattern for silicone or epoxy tooling, or metal PBF insert for a steel mould
Steps: build pattern or insert, finish the surface, fit into bolster, add cooling and ejection
For 5000 parts choose a metal insert over a soft silicone tool; state the reason
Limits: tool life, thermal conductivity of AM inserts, surface roughness of the cavity

bank.q: Compare additive manufacturing with CNC machining on tooling, material range, accuracy, production rate and cost. For what batch size and part shape is AM clearly the better choice?
outline: Subtractive: removes material, needs fixtures and tools, fast for simple large batches, wide material range, good tolerances
AM: no part-specific tooling, near-net shape, freedom for internal and lattice features, slower per part, size limits, post-processing
Cost crossover: AM fixed cost low, per-part cost high; CNC fixed cost high, per-part cost low
AM wins at low volume, complex geometry, mass customisation and single-unit spares
CNC wins at high volume, simple shapes, tight tolerance and large parts; a hybrid route is often best

bank.q: Analyse how build orientation and support structures affect build time, surface finish, strength and post-processing in SLA, FDM and powder bed fusion.
outline: Orientation fixes build height, so it fixes the number of layers and time
Orientation fixes the area of support contact and hence marks on surfaces
FDM and SLA need supports under overhangs; PBF is supported by loose powder
Layer direction is the weak direction, so loading must be considered when orienting
Trade-off between flat-on build (fast, poor bottom face) and tilted build (better finish, more supports)
Practical rule: choose the orientation that puts the critical surface vertical or upward and minimises support on functional faces

bank.q: Compare material jetting, multi-jet modelling and binder jetting for producing a full-colour architectural model, and evaluate which is most suitable.
outline: Material jetting and MJM: printhead deposits liquid photopolymer droplets, UV-cured immediately; MJM uses several heads for different colours and support
Binder jetting: printhead deposits binder into a plaster or sand powder bed; part is cured afterwards
Colour: jetting processes give true multi-colour; binder jetting gives colour on a porous, weak part
Surface and strength: cured photopolymer better than binder-glued powder
Evaluation: pick material jetting or MJM for a handled visual model, binder jetting for large cheap sand or plaster models

glossary.def: A family of processes that make a part by adding material in layers from a 3D model.
Making a part by removing material from a larger block, as in turning, milling and drilling.
A surface-only file format that represents a part as a mesh of flat triangles.
Cutting the 3D model into thin parallel cross-sections that the machine will build one by one.
The path the nozzle, laser or printhead follows inside each layer, generated by slicing software.
Temporary material built under overhangs to hold up the next layer, removed after the build.
All operations after the build, such as support removal, cleaning, curing, machining and painting.
A resin that hardens when exposed to ultraviolet light.
Chemical hardening of a resin or binder, triggered by UV light, heat or time.
A pair of small moving mirrors that steer a laser beam quickly across the resin or powder surface.
A thin spooled strand of thermoplastic, usually 1.75 mm or 2.85 mm diameter, fed to an FDM nozzle.
One straight deposited road of material; a set of parallel rasters fills a layer.
The percentage of the interior volume that is filled with material; the rest is left as air gaps.
A flat tray of loose powder, levelled thin before each layer is fused.
Heating powder particles until their surfaces bond together, without melting the whole particle.
Distance between two neighbouring scan lines of a laser inside one cross-section.
The small pool of liquid metal formed where the laser or beam strikes the material.
Metal powder carried by a gas stream through a nozzle directly into the laser melt pool.
Breaking away the cross-hatched waste block that surrounds a laminated object manufacturing part.
A criss-cross cut pattern in the waste material that makes removal easy and gives even strength.
A liquid adhesive jetted into a powder bed to glue particles into the chosen shape.
A nozzle assembly that fires small droplets of liquid material or binder on demand.
Making a mould, die, insert or pattern by AM so that production tooling arrives in days.
Direct AM production of the final part sold or used by the customer.
Producing many individually different items at close to mass-production cost, with no extra tooling per design.
